The first decisive defect occurs in the treatment of triangle LNC. Since N lies on AC, the rays CN and CA coincide, so ∠LCN=∠LCA=∠ACL=α, not α−γ. Moreover, with angles α and β at C and N, the sine law gives LN=(b/2)sinα/sin(α+β), not (b/2)sin(α−γ)/sinβ. Thus the asserted formula for cot θ_L is false and load-bearing (Rule C).

The first decisive defect is the claim that ∠LCN = α−γ. Since N lies on AC, the ray CN is exactly the ray CA, so ∠LCN = ∠LCA = α. This false load-bearing angle relation invalidates the ensuing sine-law and cotangent formulas, invoking Rule C.

The first decisive defect is the claim that symmetry under exchanging B and C forces β=γ. No argument from the angle conditions establishes β=γ. This is an unsupported central structural inference, so Rule E caps the score at 3.

The asserted “known property” expressing the alternating sorted sum as a maximum over balanced sign assignments is false. For example, for lengths 0.5, 0.3, 0.2, the alternating sum is 0.4, whereas the stated maximum is 0.5+0.3-0.2=0.6. Thus the subsequent Val_i optimization does not bound the actual payoff. This is a central invalid inference under Rule E; additionally, the incorrect final answer invokes Rule A.

The claimed characterization of the sorted alternating sum as a maximum over arbitrary sign assignments is false. For example, for lengths (0.4,0.4,0.1,0.1), the alternating sum is 0, whereas the maximum with two positive and two negative signs is 0.6. Thus the central lower-bound argument does not follow.

This makes the final classification false, so Rule A caps the score at 2.

The first score-determining defect is the false inference that, when a witness set P_i with i>N meets P(m) and H∩P_i={p}, one must have p∈P(m). The common prime in P_i∩P(m) need not belong to H. This invalidates the central finiteness argument, so Rule E caps the score at 3.

The first cap-driving defect is the inference that, if a witness set satisfies H∩P_i={p} and P_i∩P(m)≠∅, then p∈P(m). The prime in P_i∩P(m) may be a different prime omitted from H. Thus H⊆H_N∪P(m) is unsupported, so the claimed finiteness and stabilization of the sets S_n do not follow. This is a false decisive inference under Rule E, giving a ceiling of 3.

The first decisive defect is the claim that the union P of all prime divisors of the terms is finite. The asserted implication that infinitely many such primes would force some a_{n+1} to contain a prime p>a_n+M is false. For example, if a_1=2, then a_n=2n, so P contains every prime and is infinite. Thus the central finiteness argument is false and Rule E caps the score at 3.

The claimed finiteness of P is false and is the first decisive defect. For a_1=2, the rule gives a_n=2n, so every prime q occurs in a_q=2q and P is infinite. The inference that a new prime p>M forces (a_n+M)/p<2 for large n is invalid. This false claim replaces the central argument, so Rule E caps the score at 3.

The first decisive defect is the false load-bearing claim that S, the union of all prime divisors of the terms, is finite. For a_1=2, the greedy sequence is a_n=2n, so S contains every prime. This false structural inference replaces the central argument, invoking Rule E and capping the score at 3.

Step 1's claim that S is finite is false and is the first decisive defect. For example, if a_1=2, the greedy sequence is a_n=2n, so every prime divides some term and S contains all primes. The argument merely suggests that the accompanying prime q may be bounded; this is compatible with arbitrarily large p (here q=2 always). Thus the central finiteness inference fails, invoking Rule E's maximum of 3.

The first decisive defect is the unsupported claim that, after the minimum product stabilizes, only a fixed finite set of hitting sets can determine future terms. Finiteness of the minimum-product family does not imply that events with a larger hitting set can occur only finitely often: such a hitting set may intersect the persistent minimum hitting set and remove none of it, while the alternative bound m(H)≤(a_n+m*)/2 is not uniform. This is an unsupported central structural inference under Rule E, so the score is capped at 3.

The first decisive defect is the unsupported inference that stabilization of the minimum hitting-set product implies that all future steps are determined by a fixed finite family of hitting sets of bounded product. The claim that the case a_{n+1}=m(H)>m^* can occur only finitely often does not follow from finiteness of \mathcal M_n and is false: for the admissible sequence 2,4,6,8,\ldots, the full prime support H=P_{n+1} gives m(H)=a_{n+1}>2 for infinitely many squarefree terms while removing no minimum hitting set. This leaves the central finiteness assertion unproved, so Rule E caps the score at 3.

The decisive induction step is invalid: W_{n,p} is defined from an arbitrary subcollection of the original prime-support sets and is not associated with any sequence satisfying the same greedy rule with an initial term having k-1 prime factors. Thus the inductive hypothesis cannot be applied. This leaves eventual stabilization of V_n—the central structural claim—unproved, so Rule E caps the score at 3.

Rule E applies at the inductive step: the induction hypothesis concerns V-sets arising from a sequence satisfying the original greedy rule, but W_{n,p} comes merely from a subcollection of the supports S_i. No sequence satisfying that rule, with an initial term having at most k-1 prime factors, is constructed. Thus the asserted stabilization of W_{n,p}, and hence of V_n, is unsupported.

The first decisive defect is the claimed bound that every inclusion-minimal hitting set of \(\mathcal G_n\) has size at most \(|\mathcal P(a_1)|\) merely because \(\mathcal P(a_1)\) is itself a hitting set. This implication is false in general and does not establish the bounded-rank premise needed for stabilization. Thus the central stabilization argument is unsupported, invoking Rule E and capping the score at 3.

The claimed uniform bound on the sizes of members of \(\mathcal G_n\) is false. For the admissible start \(a_1=35\), one gets \(a_2=40\) and \(a_3=42\), so \(m=2\) but \(\mathcal G_3=\{\{5,7\},\{2,5\},\{2,3,7\}\}\) contains a 3-element set. In particular, the assertion that every member of \(\mathcal G_n\) is a minimal hitting set of \(\mathcal G_{n-1}\) is false (for example, \(\{5,7\}\) is not minimal because \(\{5\}\) already hits \(\mathcal G_2\)). This is a false load-bearing assertion under Rule C, and because it removes the central stabilization argument, Rule E's ceiling of 3 applies.

The first decisive defect is the unsupported claim that the whole family M_n must stabilize. An inclusion-minimal hitting set need not have size at most that of another hitting set: for Q_1={2,3}, Q_2={2,5}, Q_3={2,7}, the set {3,5,7} is an inclusion-minimal hitting set larger than Q_1. Moreover, boundedness of the minimum element of M_n gives no bound such as m·p ≤ ∏_{p∈Q_1}p for all other minimal hitting sets. Thus stabilization of m_min(n) does not imply stabilization of M_n. This is an unsupported central structural inference, invoking Rule E and capping the score at 3.

The first decisive defect is the false claim that every inclusion-minimal hitting set of \(\mathcal F_n\) has size at most \(|Q_1|\). For the admissible start \(a_1=35\), the greedy sequence begins \(35,40,42,45\), with supports \(\{5,7\},\{2,5\},\{2,3,7\},\{3,5\}\). Then \(\{2,3,7\}\) is a minimal hitting set of size 3, whereas \(|Q_1|=2\). Thus the claimed bound, and likewise the asserted product bound by \(\prod_{p\in Q_1}p\), is false.

The decisive claim that every syndetic set which is an intersection of periodic sets must itself be periodic is false. For example, 6Z union {2} is syndetic and equals the intersection over r of the periodic sets 6Z union (2+r!Z), but it has no positive period. Thus Rule E applies: the central periodicity inference is invalid, giving a maximum score of 3.

The decisive step claiming that every syndetic intersection of periodic sets is periodic is false. For example, as a subset of the positive integers, 2ℤ∪{1} has bounded gaps and equals an intersection of periodic sets, but has no positive period. Thus the argument does not establish that M is periodic. This is an unsupported and false central inference, so Rule E caps the score at 3.
